title: How Much Alcohol Is in Kombucha? Store, Hard, and Homemade
excerpt: Store kombucha stays under 0.5% alcohol, hard kombucha runs about 4-7%, and homebrew is unpredictable. What that means for getting drunk, breath tests, pregnancy, and hangovers.
metaDescription: How much alcohol is in kombucha? Store-bought stays under 0.5% ABV, hard kombucha runs 4-7%, homebrew varies. What it means for tests and hangovers.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** regular store-bought kombucha has a small amount of alcohol, and in the US it's meant to stay **below 0.5% alcohol by volume (ABV)**. That's about the same as many "non-alcoholic" beers and far too little to get an adult drunk. Hard kombucha is a different product: it's brewed on purpose to be a real alcoholic drink, usually somewhere around **4% to 7% ABV**, which puts it in the same range as beer. Homemade kombucha sits in between and is the hardest to predict, because nobody is testing it, and it often ends up above 0.5%.

**The quick version by type:**

| Type of kombucha | Typical alcohol content | Legally an alcoholic drink (US)? |
|---|---|---|
| Store-bought (regular, non-alcoholic) | Under 0.5% ABV, often lower | No, as long as it stays under 0.5% |
| Hard kombucha (sold next to beer and seltzer) | Usually about 4% to 7% ABV, some higher | Yes, ID required |
| Homebrewed kombucha | Unknown; often around 0.5% to 1%, sometimes higher with long or warm ferments | Not regulated, but can be alcoholic |

So if you're asking because you want to know whether a bottle of GT's or Health-Ade will show up on a breath test, affect a medication, or count as "drinking," the answer is: it contains a trace, it's not zero, and whether that trace matters depends on why you're asking. This guide walks through each case.

> **A note on health situations.** This article is general information, not medical advice. If you are pregnant, take a medicine that reacts with any amount of alcohol (such as disulfiram or metronidazole), have liver disease, or avoid alcohol completely for any personal or health reason, ask your doctor or pharmacist whether trace-alcohol drinks like kombucha are okay for you. Hard kombucha is a full-strength alcoholic drink and carries all the same risks as beer.

## Why Kombucha Has Alcohol at All

Kombucha is sweetened tea fermented by a SCOBY, which stands for "symbiotic culture of bacteria and yeast." It's the rubbery disc you may have seen floating in a jar. The fermentation happens in two linked steps:

1. **Yeast eats the sugar and makes alcohol.** This is the same basic process that makes beer and wine. The yeast in the culture converts sugar into ethanol (drinking alcohol) and carbon dioxide.
2. **Bacteria eat the alcohol and make acids.** Acetic acid bacteria, the same kind that turn wine into vinegar, convert much of that ethanol into acetic acid and other organic acids. That's where kombucha gets its sour, slightly vinegary bite.

Because the second step keeps eating what the first step makes, alcohol in kombucha normally stays low. But the balance is never perfect. Some ethanol is always present at any given moment, and if conditions favor the yeast over the bacteria, the level climbs. Warm temperatures, extra sugar, sealed bottles with little oxygen (acetic acid bacteria need oxygen to work), and long fermentation times can all tip things toward more alcohol.

That's the core reason kombucha can't be guaranteed to be alcohol-free. It's a living, fermenting drink, and the alcohol is a natural by-product rather than an ingredient someone added.

## How Much Alcohol Is in Store-Bought Kombucha?

In the United States, the line between a soft drink and an alcoholic beverage is **0.5% ABV**. A fermented drink that stays under that line is regulated like food by the FDA. Once it reaches 0.5% or more at any point, it becomes an alcoholic beverage under federal law, which brings in the Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau (TTB), alcohol taxes, labeling rules, and age restrictions.

Regular kombucha brands sold in the refrigerated section of grocery stores are made to stay under that limit. Producers use different methods to keep alcohol down, including controlling fermentation carefully, filtering or diluting the finished brew, using cultures that make less alcohol, and in some cases removing alcohol after brewing. Many brands say their products test well below 0.5%.

A few practical points:

- **"Non-alcoholic" doesn't mean zero.** Under US rules, "non-alcoholic" can be used on drinks under 0.5% ABV. Only "alcohol-free" is supposed to mean no detectable alcohol, and you will rarely see kombucha described that way.
- **The level can rise after bottling.** Because kombucha is often raw and unpasteurized, the live culture can keep fermenting in the bottle. That's why bottles carry "keep refrigerated" warnings. A bottle left warm in a car or on a counter for days can build up more alcohol than it had when it left the brewery. The TTB has published guidance for kombucha makers that specifically warns about alcohol increasing after bottling.
- **This has caused real problems before.** In 2010, kombucha was pulled from many store shelves, including at Whole Foods, after testing found some bottles above the 0.5% limit. Several major brands reformulated afterward, and some briefly sold higher-alcohol versions as separate, age-restricted products.

### How much alcohol is that, really?

Percentages are abstract, so here's the math in drinks. A US "standard drink" contains about 14 grams of pure alcohol, roughly the amount in a 12-ounce beer at 5%, a 5-ounce glass of wine, or a 1.5-ounce shot of spirits.

A 16-ounce bottle of kombucha at the very top of the legal range (0.5%) contains a little under 2 grams of alcohol. That works out to roughly **one-seventh of a standard drink**. Put another way, you'd need to drink around seven 16-ounce bottles at the upper limit to take in as much alcohol as one regular beer, and you'd be drinking them over the same time you'd drink a beer. Most bottles sit below the limit, so the real number is usually smaller still.

Your liver clears alcohol at roughly one standard drink per hour for an average adult. A fraction of a drink spread over the time it takes to finish a bottle is processed quickly, which is why a bottle of regular kombucha won't make a healthy adult feel drunk.

### How it compares to other everyday foods

Trace alcohol isn't unique to kombucha. Small amounts of ethanol naturally show up in many fermented or very ripe foods. Studies that have measured everyday foods have found traces in things like fruit juices, very ripe bananas, some breads and burger buns, kefir, and soy sauce. Non-alcoholic beer is also allowed up to 0.5% in the US.

This doesn't mean those foods are "alcoholic." It means your body handles tiny amounts of ethanol routinely, and store kombucha sits in that same low tier as long as it's kept cold and stays within its label.

## How Much Alcohol Is in Hard Kombucha?

Hard kombucha is a deliberately alcoholic product. Brewers either let fermentation run further with extra sugar and yeast, or they ferment a kombucha base and then do a second, beer-style fermentation to push the alcohol up. It's sold next to craft beer and hard seltzer, carries an alcohol percentage on the can, and requires ID to buy.

Most hard kombuchas land somewhere around **4% to 7% ABV**, with some brands going higher. That's right in beer territory. Always check the can, because strength varies a lot between brands and even between flavors from the same brand.

Here's what common strengths mean in standard drinks:

| Can size and strength | Approximate standard drinks |
|---|---|
| 12 oz at 4.5% ABV | About 0.9 |
| 12 oz at 6% ABV | About 1.2 |
| 12 oz at 7% ABV | About 1.4 |
| 16 oz "tallboy" at 7% ABV | About 1.9 |

That last row is worth noticing. A single tallboy of stronger hard kombucha is close to two standard drinks. If you're counting your drinks, count a tallboy as two.

### The health-halo problem with hard kombucha

Hard kombucha is often marketed with words like "gut-friendly," "live cultures," "organic," and "lower sugar." Some of those things may be true about a particular product. None of them changes what the alcohol does in your body.

- **Alcohol is alcohol.** Ethanol from hard kombucha is metabolized exactly like ethanol from beer, wine, or vodka. It raises your blood alcohol level the same way, impairs driving the same way, and can cause a hangover the same way.
- **Probiotic claims are shaky in alcoholic versions.** Some hard kombuchas are pasteurized or filtered, which reduces or removes live cultures. Even where cultures remain, there's no good evidence that the small amounts in a can offset the effects of alcohol on your gut. Alcohol itself is known to disrupt the gut lining and gut bacteria, which our article on [how alcohol affects your gut microbiome](/never-hungover/how-alcohol-affects-your-gut-microbiome-the-hidden-health-impact-2025) covers in more detail.
- **"Easy drinking" can mean faster drinking.** Hard kombucha is tart, fizzy, and often fruity, which can make it go down faster than you'd drink a beer. Faster drinking means a higher peak blood alcohol level and, usually, a worse next morning.

If you like hard kombucha, there's nothing wrong with choosing it because you prefer the taste. Just treat it like the beer-strength drink it is.

### Does hard kombucha give you a worse hangover?

There's no good research comparing hangovers from hard kombucha with hangovers from beer or seltzer specifically. What we know about hangovers in general points to a few things that matter more than the drink's "health" branding:

- **Total alcohol** is the biggest factor. More drinks, worse hangover, regardless of the type.
- **Speed of drinking** matters. Easy-drinking, fizzy drinks can be finished fast, and carbonation may speed up how quickly alcohol is absorbed.
- **Sugar and acidity** may add to stomach upset for some people, though this is less established.
- **Congeners**, the by-products of fermentation that give drinks flavor, are linked to worse hangovers in some studies of darker spirits. Hard kombucha is a fermented drink with plenty of flavor compounds, but no one has studied its congener profile against hangovers.

The same habits that help with any drink apply here. Our guide to the [hard seltzer hangover](/never-hungover/hard-seltzer-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) covers the "light, fizzy drink that still wrecks you" problem in more depth, and most of it applies to hard kombucha too.

## How Much Alcohol Is in Homemade Kombucha?

Homebrewed kombucha is the least predictable of the three. Without lab testing, you don't know your alcohol level, and home conditions often favor more alcohol than commercial brewing does.

Things that tend to raise alcohol in homebrew:

- **Second fermentation in sealed bottles.** Many people bottle their kombucha with fruit or juice to make it fizzy. That adds sugar, and the sealed bottle cuts off oxygen, so yeast keeps making alcohol while the acid bacteria slow down. This is the step most likely to push homebrew over 0.5%.
- **Warm rooms.** Yeast speeds up in warmth. A summer kitchen can produce a noticeably stronger batch than a cool one.
- **Extra sugar or sweet fruit.** More sugar is more fuel for alcohol.
- **Longer ferments.** The longer a sealed bottle sits warm before refrigeration, the more alcohol it can build.

Studies and lab tests of homebrewed kombucha have found a wide range, with many samples landing above 0.5% and some reaching 1% to 3% or more. Very sour, flat batches fermented open to the air tend to be lower in alcohol, because the bacteria have had time to convert it to acid.

If you homebrew and want to keep alcohol down:

- Keep the first ferment in an open jar covered with cloth, not sealed.
- Keep second ferments short, and refrigerate the bottles once they're fizzy enough.
- Don't add more sugar or fruit than you need for flavor.
- Treat your homebrew as possibly mildly alcoholic, especially if it's going to kids, someone who is pregnant, or someone who doesn't drink.

Home hydrometers, the floating gauges beer brewers use, are not reliable for measuring alcohol in kombucha, because the acids and leftover sugars throw off the reading. If you truly need to know the number, only a lab test will tell you.

## Can Kombucha Get You Drunk?

**Regular store-bought kombucha:** realistically, no. At under 0.5%, a healthy adult would need to drink several large bottles quickly to take in even one standard drink's worth of alcohol, and their body would be clearing it the whole time. Most people would be uncomfortably full of fizzy, acidic tea long before they felt anything from the alcohol.

Some people do say they feel "a little buzzed" after kombucha. That can come from a few places that aren't alcohol: caffeine from the tea, a quick hit of sugar, or simply expectation. It's also possible that a warm or old bottle had fermented above its labeled level.

**Hard kombucha:** yes, exactly like beer. Two or three cans can put many adults over the legal driving limit, depending on body size, food, and how fast they drink.

**Homebrew:** usually not, but it's harder to say. A strong batch at 2% to 3% is about half the strength of a light beer, so a few large glasses could add up to a real drink's worth of alcohol.

## Will Kombucha Show Up on a Breathalyzer or Alcohol Test?

This is one of the most common reasons people ask about kombucha, so here's what's generally true.

- **Breath tests right after drinking.** Any drink with alcohol, including kombucha, can leave a tiny amount of alcohol in your mouth for a few minutes. A breath test taken immediately afterward could pick up a brief, false reading from that "mouth alcohol." This is the reason police breath-testing procedures usually include a waiting period of around 15 to 20 minutes before the test. Once that clears, a bottle of regular kombucha is very unlikely to produce a meaningful reading.
- **Blood alcohol level.** The amount of alcohol in a bottle of regular kombucha is too small to raise blood alcohol meaningfully in a healthy adult. It won't put you anywhere near a legal driving limit.
- **Hard kombucha** will show up exactly like beer, because it is a beer-strength drink.
- **Strict abstinence tests are different.** Some monitoring programs use very sensitive urine tests that look for alcohol breakdown products (such as EtG, ethyl glucuronide) rather than alcohol itself. These tests can detect very small exposures, and the people running them often tell participants to avoid all sources of trace alcohol, including kombucha, non-alcoholic beer, and even some mouthwashes and hand sanitizers. If you're in any program that tests for alcohol, ask the program directly before drinking kombucha. Don't assume "non-alcoholic" will be accepted as an explanation.

## Who Should Think Twice About Kombucha's Alcohol

For most healthy adults, the trace alcohol in store kombucha isn't a meaningful concern. A few groups have good reason to be more careful.

**People who are pregnant or breastfeeding.** No safe level of alcohol during pregnancy has been established, and major health bodies advise avoiding alcohol entirely. The trace in store kombucha is small, but because it can vary and rise after bottling, and because raw kombucha is unpasteurized, many doctors suggest skipping it or asking first. Homebrew and hard kombucha are clearly off the table. Our guide on [pregnancy and alcohol](/never-hungover/pregnant-women-and-alcohol-complete-fetal-impact-guide-2025) covers the broader picture.

**People taking medicines that react with any alcohol.** Disulfiram (Antabuse) is designed to cause a strong reaction to even small amounts of alcohol, and its labeling warns about hidden sources like sauces, vinegars, and some cough syrups. The antibiotic metronidazole and a few related drugs also carry warnings about alcohol. If you take one of these, ask your pharmacist about kombucha before you drink it.

**Kids.** Store kombucha's trace alcohol is similar to some juices, but kombucha is also acidic, often caffeinated, and sometimes high in sugar. Many pediatric sources suggest limiting it for young children. Homemade and hard kombucha shouldn't be given to children.

**People who avoid alcohol for personal, religious, or health reasons.** If your goal is zero alcohol, regular kombucha isn't zero. Whether a trace like this matters to you is a personal decision. Some people are comfortable with it, the same way they're comfortable with ripe fruit or bread. Others prefer to avoid fermented drinks entirely, or pick kombucha brands that say they remove alcohol after brewing.

**People with liver disease or a weakened immune system.** For people whose doctors have told them to avoid alcohol completely, or who are immunocompromised (raw, unpasteurized drinks carry a small infection risk), it's worth asking a doctor before drinking kombucha regularly.

## Is Kombucha Good for a Hangover?

Kombucha shows up on a lot of "hangover cure" lists. Here's an honest look.

**What it might help with:**

- **Fluid.** It's mostly water, so it helps you rehydrate, though plain water does that just as well.
- **Some quick sugar.** A bit of sugar can help if you feel shaky after drinking. Plain fruit juice or toast does the same.
- **A little caffeine.** Kombucha is made from tea, so it contains some caffeine, usually less than a cup of coffee. That can take the edge off a caffeine-withdrawal headache for regular coffee drinkers.

**What it probably won't do:**

- There's **no good evidence that kombucha treats or prevents hangovers**. No clinical trials have tested it for that.
- Probiotic claims are based on the general idea that alcohol upsets your gut. That part is real, but there's no evidence that one bottle of kombucha the next morning undoes it. If you're curious about the probiotic angle, our article on [probiotics for hangovers](/never-hungover/hangover-probiotics) looks at what the research actually shows.
- It's acidic and fizzy, which can make an already irritated stomach feel worse. If you have heartburn or nausea, kombucha may not be the best choice.

**The "hair of the dog" question.** Regular kombucha's trace alcohol is far too small to act as hair of the dog, which is a bad strategy anyway because it only delays the hangover. Drinking hard kombucha the next morning is just more drinking.

If you enjoy kombucha and it settles your stomach, it's a fine choice for the morning after. Just don't expect it to fix anything that water, food, and sleep wouldn't.

## How to Read a Kombucha Label

A quick checklist when you're standing in the store:

- **Where is it shelved?** Regular kombucha sits in the refrigerated drinks section. Hard kombucha sits with beer, wine, and seltzer, and the register will ask for ID.
- **Is there an ABV percentage on the label?** Hard kombucha must state its alcohol content. Regular kombucha usually doesn't list a number, and may say "non-alcoholic" or include a note about trace alcohol from fermentation.
- **Does it say "raw" or "unpasteurized"?** Raw kombucha is more likely to keep fermenting if it gets warm, so keep it cold.
- **Is there a government warning?** In the US, alcoholic beverages (0.5% and above) must carry the federal health warning about pregnancy and driving. If you see it, you're holding an alcoholic drink.
- **Is the bottle swollen or extra fizzy?** A bottle that's been warm and built up a lot of pressure has probably kept fermenting. It may be a bit higher in alcohol than labeled.

## Kombucha vs. Other "Low-Alcohol" Drinks

Here's how kombucha fits among other drinks people often ask about:

| Drink | Typical alcohol |
|---|---|
| Store-bought kombucha | Under 0.5% ABV |
| Non-alcoholic beer | Under 0.5% ABV in the US (some are 0.0%) |
| Kefir (milk or water kefir) | Trace amounts, varies with fermentation |
| Homebrewed kombucha | Often 0.5% to 1%, sometimes higher |
| Light beer | About 4% ABV |
| Hard kombucha | About 4% to 7% ABV, some higher |
| Hard seltzer | Usually about 4% to 6% ABV |
| Regular beer | About 5% ABV |
| Wine | About 11% to 14% ABV |

Labeling rules also vary by country. In the UK, for example, "alcohol-free" is meant for drinks at or below 0.05% ABV, while "low alcohol" covers drinks up to 1.2%. If you're traveling or buying imported kombucha, the label terms may not mean exactly what they mean in the US.

## If You're Drinking Hard Kombucha: Keep the Next Morning Manageable

If you're choosing hard kombucha for a night out, the same basic rules apply as for any beer-strength drink:

- **Count tallboys as two drinks** if they're 6% or stronger.
- **Pace yourself.** Fizzy, tart drinks go down fast. Try alternating with water.
- **Eat beforehand.** Food in your stomach slows alcohol absorption.
- **Know when you're done.** The surest way to avoid a hangover is to drink less.

Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through the habits with the best evidence behind them.

Some people also take DHM (dihydromyricetin), a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree, before or while drinking. Most of the research on DHM comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data, so think of it as promising rather than proven. There is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers on its own, and it doesn't lower your blood alcohol or make it safe to drive. If you want to try it alongside sensible drinking, [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is a budget-friendly single-ingredient option, and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) adds other ingredients like L-cysteine. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when. None of this applies to regular kombucha, which doesn't contain enough alcohol to need any of it.

## The Bottom Line

- **Store-bought kombucha** contains a trace of alcohol from fermentation and is meant to stay under 0.5% ABV in the US. That's about one-seventh of a standard drink per 16-ounce bottle at most, and usually less. It won't get a healthy adult drunk.
- **Hard kombucha** is a real alcoholic drink, usually around 4% to 7% ABV. Treat it like beer, including for driving and hangovers. Health-focused marketing doesn't change what the alcohol does.
- **Homemade kombucha** is unpredictable and often ends up above 0.5%, especially after a sealed, sugary second fermentation in a warm room.
- **Keep regular kombucha cold.** Warm bottles can keep fermenting and gain alcohol.
- **Ask first if you need zero alcohol.** That includes pregnancy, certain medications like disulfiram or metronidazole, and alcohol-monitoring programs.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does kombucha have alcohol in it?**

Yes. All kombucha contains some alcohol, because yeast in the culture turns sugar into ethanol during fermentation. In regular store-bought kombucha, the amount is kept below 0.5% alcohol by volume in the US, which is the same limit used for non-alcoholic beer. Hard kombucha is brewed to be alcoholic, usually around 4% to 7% ABV.

**How much alcohol is in a bottle of GT's, Health-Ade, or other store kombucha?**

Regular kombucha sold in the refrigerated section of US stores is meant to stay under 0.5% ABV, and many brands say theirs tests well below that. A 16-ounce bottle at the full 0.5% limit holds a little under 2 grams of alcohol, roughly one-seventh of a standard drink. Check the brand's label or website for their specific claims, and keep bottles refrigerated, since warm bottles can keep fermenting.

**Can you get drunk from kombucha?**

Not from regular store-bought kombucha. You would need to drink several large bottles quickly to take in even one standard drink's worth of alcohol, and your body clears it as you go. Hard kombucha is different: it's about as strong as beer, and a few cans can impair you and put you over the legal driving limit.

**How much alcohol is in hard kombucha?**

Most hard kombuchas are around 4% to 7% ABV, and some are stronger. A 12-ounce can at 6% is about 1.2 standard drinks, and a 16-ounce can at 7% is close to two. The exact percentage is printed on the can, and it can vary between flavors from the same brand.

**Does homemade kombucha have more alcohol than store-bought?**

Often, yes. Homebrewed kombucha isn't tested, and the common home step of bottling with fruit or juice for a second fermentation adds sugar and cuts off oxygen, which favors alcohol. Warm rooms and long ferments push it higher. Many homebrews end up above 0.5%, and some reach 1% to 3% or more.

**Will drinking kombucha make me fail a breathalyzer?**

Regular kombucha won't raise your blood alcohol enough to matter, but any drink with alcohol can leave a trace in your mouth for a few minutes, which can briefly affect a breath test taken right away. Standard testing procedures include a waiting period to rule that out. Hard kombucha will register like beer. If you're in a program with sensitive alcohol testing, ask the program before drinking kombucha.

**Is kombucha safe during pregnancy?**

Many doctors suggest avoiding it or asking first. Store kombucha has only a trace of alcohol, but no safe level of alcohol in pregnancy has been established, the amount can rise if a bottle gets warm, and raw kombucha is unpasteurized. Hard kombucha and homebrew should be avoided. Talk to your doctor or midwife about what's right for you.

**Is kombucha good for a hangover?**

There is no good evidence that kombucha treats or prevents hangovers. It can help with fluids, and it has a little sugar and caffeine, which some people find helpful the morning after. But it's acidic and fizzy, which can upset an irritated stomach, and its probiotic content hasn't been shown to undo alcohol's effects on the gut. Water, food, and rest do most of the work.

**Can kids drink kombucha?**

Store-bought kombucha has trace alcohol in the same general range as some fruit juices, but it's also acidic, often caffeinated, and can be high in sugar, so many pediatric sources suggest limiting it for young children. Homemade and hard kombucha should not be given to children.
